top_choice_rationale: P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore, B006) recognises one well-bounded, roughly thirty-year-old mechanism. Borrowing limits depend on collateral values, and collateral values depend on borrowing, so small shocks become large and persistent credit cycles. It explains why the pattern arises, not just that it exists. The 2007-09 crisis and the later literature have tested it, and it is now part of the shared core of macro-finance and central-bank modelling. Attribution is the cleanest on the slate, because no one disputes the originators. The pair also avoids re-crediting the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator, and I could not name a separable Gertler contribution that is distinct from the 2022 banking theme. The main reservations are adjacency to the 2022 prize, which a narrow collateral-amplification citation can address, and mixed direct identification of the specific collateral channel. P002 (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) is a close second, with a compact credit core and a longer applied record. Its cost is the visible omission of Bresnahan and Reiss. P003 (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) is third. It is strong on empirical design, but it joins technology and trade strands and overlaps with recent labour prizes. P000 is last, since several mature, well-attributed candidates exist. This ranking rests on background knowledge, not verified citation data.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile. No documented connection to Kiyotaki, Moore, Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes, Autor, Dorn or Hanson. I disclose, without adjudicating, a Lund collegial tie to Tommy Andersson, who supports P002. My field of economic history is distant from all three proposals.
